docs.title: 🛡️ Defensive Engineering Standards
docs.text:
Every investigation follows the same structure as a SOC ticket:

  1. Initial Trigger & Scope: Documenting the alert provenance, affected host, and user context.
  2. Forensic Telemetry: Raw Sysmon logs, PCAPs, or mail headers, with the queries used to pull them. Raw files live in the repo's evidence/ folder.
  3. Timeline & Pivoting: Reconstructing chronological attacker execution steps.
  4. Verdict: True or false positive, severity, and escalation call.
  5. Detection: A rule that catches it next time, tested against the lab data where possible.

docs.title: Suspicious LSASS Memory Access (Splunk SPL)
docs.text:
Filters on Sysmon Event ID 10 where the target is lsass.exe and the access mask includes memory read permissions (0x1fffff, 0x1010, 0x1410), excluding core system processes.

index=botsv1 "<EventID>10</EventID>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='SourceImage'>(?<SourceImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='TargetImage'>(?<TargetImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='GrantedAccess'>(?<GrantedAccess>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Computer>(?<host_name>[^<]+)</Computer>"
| where match(TargetImage, "(?i)\\\\lsass\.exe$")
| where match(GrantedAccess, "(?i)^0x(1fffff|1010|1410|1438|143a|1f3fff)$")
| where NOT match(SourceImage, "(?i)^C:\\\\Windows\\\\System32\\\\(svchost|wininit|csrss|services|lsm)\.exe$")
| eval severity=if(match(SourceImage, "(?i)\\\\(AppData|Temp|Users\\\\Public)\\\\"), "critical", "high")
| stats count min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen values(GrantedAccess) as access by host_name SourceImage severity
| sort - count
View Sigma Rule Definition 
title: Suspicious Process Access to LSASS Memory
status: experimental
author: Mian Talha Nayyar
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1003.001
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: process_access
detection:
  selection:
    TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    GrantedAccess:
      - '0x1fffff'
      - '0x1010'
      - '0x1410'
      - '0x1438'
      - '0x143a'
      - '0x1f3fff'
  filter_system:
    SourceImage:
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe'
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\wininit.exe'
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\csrss.exe'
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\services.exe'
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\lsm.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_system
falsepositives:
  - EDR and antivirus monitoring agents
  - Legitimate administrator memory dumps via Task Manager
level: high

docs.title: Office Application Spawning Command Shell (Splunk SPL)
docs.text:
Detects living-off-the-land techniques where Microsoft Office applications spawn command interpreters (cmd.exe, powershell.exe) indicative of macro exploitation.

index=wineventlog EventCode=4688
| eval parent=lower(Creator_Process_Name), child=lower(New_Process_Name)
| where match(parent, "\\\\(winword|excel|powerpnt|outlook|onenote)\.exe$")
    AND match(child, "\\\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32)\.exe$")
| table _time host Account_Name parent child Process_Command_Line

docs.title: Outbound Cleartext HTTP from Internal Workstation (Splunk SPL)
docs.text:
Isolates direct outbound cleartext HTTP (port 80) connections originating from endpoints using non-standard or scripted user agents.

index=proxy dest_port=80
| where NOT match(http_user_agent, "(?i)(mozilla|windows-update|microsoft)")
| stats count values(url) as urls dc(dest) as destinations by src http_user_agent
| where count > 5

docs.title: Lab 01: Windows Process Creation Auditing (Event ID 4688)
docs.text:
Category: Endpoint Telemetry and Baselining ATT&CK: T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter | T1204.002 User Execution: Malicious File Tools: Local Security Policy, Windows Event Viewer Host: Windows 10/11 lab workstation (DESKTOP-2UVTUII)

Verdict: Benign | Baseline established

The process captured (services.exe launching svchost.exe as SYSTEM) is normal Windows service startup. The value of this lab is the baseline and the detection logic it produced.

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
Attackers lean on built-in Windows binaries to run commands, enumerate the host, and launch payloads. Windows does not log process creation by default, so without it a SOC is blind to most of that activity.

The goal: turn on process creation auditing, generate telemetry, and learn to read Event ID 4688 for parent-child process lineage.

docs.title: 2. Configuration
docs.text:
1. Opened secpol.msc and went to Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > System Audit Policies > Detailed Tracking.
  2. Enabled Audit Process Creation for Success and Failure.
  3. Filtered the Security log in Event Viewer to Event ID 4688.

Gap found: command lines are off by default

4688 only records the binary name unless you also enable Administrative Templates > System > Audit Process Creation > Include command line in process creation events. Without it you can see powershell.exe ran, but not the encoded payload it ran. This is the first setting I'd check in any new environment.

docs.title: A single 4688 event
docs.text: Field Value Meaning Event ID 4688 A new process was created Creator account SYSTEM (DESKTOP-2UVTUII$) Launched by the OS itself New process C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe The child Creator process C:\Windows\System32\services.exe The parent Mandatory label System Mandatory Level Highest integrity

docs.title: 4. Analysis
docs.text:
Process lineage is the core of endpoint triage. The question is never just "what ran" but "what launched it".

Parent Child Read services.exe svchost.exe Normal. This is how Windows starts services explorer.exe chrome.exe Normal. User opened a browser winword.exe powershell.exe Malicious until proven otherwise. Classic macro execution excel.exe cmd.exe Malicious until proven otherwise. Same pattern wmiprvse.exe powershell.exe Suspicious. Common in remote WMI execution

docs.title: 5. Detection Logic
docs.text:
Office applications should almost never start a shell. This SPL flags it from Windows Security logs:

index=wineventlog EventCode=4688
| eval parent=lower(Creator_Process_Name), child=lower(New_Process_Name)
| where match(parent, "\\\\(winword|excel|powerpnt|outlook|onenote)\.exe$")
    AND match(child, "\\\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32)\.exe$")
| table _time host Account_Name parent child Process_Command_Line

Status

Logic only. Next step is to trigger it with an Atomic Red Team macro test and record the results here.

docs.title: 6. Takeaways
docs.text:
• Know the baseline first. svchost.exe is normal. svchost.exe launched by anything other than services.exe is not.
  • Enable command line logging. Process names without arguments leave the most important evidence out.
  • Sysmon Event ID 1 is the upgrade. It adds hashes, parent command lines, and process GUIDs, which is what Lab 03 relies on.

docs.title: Lab 02: Network Traffic Analysis and HTTP Stream Reconstruction
docs.text:
Category: Network Forensics ATT&CK: T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols | TA0011 Command and Control Tools: Wireshark (Protocol Hierarchy, Endpoints, Follow TCP Stream) Evidence: http.cap (public Wireshark sample capture)

Verdict: Benign in this capture | Pattern worth alerting on

The session is a terminal browser pulling a public directory listing. Nothing malicious was downloaded, but cleartext HTTP from a non-standard client is exactly what C2 and scripted downloads look like on the wire.

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text: When endpoint logs are missing or wiped, packets are still the source of truth. The goal: triage a capture, isolate application-layer requests, rebuild the full session, and pull out the artifacts an analyst would put in a ticket.

docs.title: 2. Method
docs.text:
1. Scoped the capture. Used Statistics > Protocol Hierarchy for the protocol mix and Statistics > Endpoints (IPv6) for who talked to whom.
  2. Filtered to requests. Applied http.request to drop transport noise and keep only client-initiated web requests.
  3. Rebuilt the session. Used Follow > TCP Stream to read the request and response as one conversation.

Useful filters for this kind of triage:

http.request                              # client requests only
http.request and !(http.user_agent contains "Mozilla")   # non-browser clients
http.response.code >= 400                 # errors and blocked requests
tcp.port == 80 and ip.src == <internal>   # cleartext traffic leaving a host

docs.title: Reconstructed TCP stream
docs.text: Artifact Value Frame 49 Client 2001:6f8:102d:0:2d0:9ff:fee3:e8de (source port 59201) Server 2001:6f8:900:7c0::2 port 80 Host header cl-1985.ham-01.de.sixxs.net User-Agent Lynx/2.8.6rel.2 libwww-FM/2.14 SSL-MM/1.4.1 OpenSSL/0.9.8b Response HTTP/1.1 200 OK from Apache, open directory listing

docs.title: 4. Analysis
docs.text:
• Everything is readable. Over port 80 with no TLS, the headers, client identity, and full response are exposed. Any credentials sent here would be too.
  • The client is not a normal browser. Lynx is a terminal browser. On a corporate workstation, a non-standard User-Agent usually means a script, a tool, or something running without a user at the keyboard.
  • Open directory listing. The server exposed .pdf and .htm files. In a real case I'd carve anything downloaded with File > Export Objects > HTTP, hash it, and check the hash against threat intel.

docs.title: 5. Detection Logic
docs.text:
Cleartext outbound HTTP from workstations with an unusual User-Agent, using proxy or Zeek-style HTTP logs:

index=proxy dest_port=80
| where NOT match(http_user_agent, "(?i)(mozilla|windows-update|microsoft)")
| stats count values(url) as urls dc(dest) as destinations by src http_user_agent
| where count > 5

Status

Logic only. Next step is to run it against a capture with real beaconing (planned for Lab 07).

docs.title: 6. Takeaways
docs.text:
• Port 80 leaving a workstation is worth a look. Almost all legitimate web traffic is TLS now.
  • User-Agent is cheap context. It's not proof, since attackers can fake it, but an odd one is a fast way to prioritize.
  • Follow the stream. Single packets are fragments. The stream is what goes in the report.

docs.title: Lab 03: Threat Hunting LSASS Credential Dumping in Splunk
docs.text:
Category: SIEM Threat Hunting and Detection Engineering ATT&CK: T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory | TA0006 Credential Access Tools: Splunk Enterprise, SPL, Sysmon (Event IDs 1, 10, 11) Evidence: windows-sysmon.log (7,974 events) | Detection: detections/

Verdict: True Positive | Critical | Escalate to IR

Two domain controllers had LSASS memory dumped with six different methods, including a renamed binary built to evade name-based detection. Domain credentials should be treated as compromised.

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
lsass.exe holds credentials, Kerberos tickets, and NTLM hashes in memory. Dumping it is how attackers move from one compromised host to the whole domain.

The goal: ingest raw Sysmon telemetry into Splunk, separate attack activity from normal system noise, rebuild the attack timeline, and ship a detection that does not depend on tool names.

docs.title: 2. Data Source
docs.text:
Field Value Telemetry Sysmon Operational log, raw XML Key events 10 ProcessAccess, 1 ProcessCreate, 11 FileCreate Hosts win-dc-807.attackrange.local, win-dc-262.attackrange.local Event time range 2020-11-03 to 2021-02-03 (UTC) Adversary simulation Atomic Red Team T1003.001, run in Splunk Attack Range

Index name

I loaded the log into a local Splunk index named botsv1. The data itself is Attack Range telemetry, not the BOTS v1 dataset.

docs.title: Step 1: Broad sweep
docs.text:
Every event mentioning LSASS, as source or target:

index=botsv1 "lsass.exe"

Result: 851 events. Too broad to triage, since LSASS also appears as the source of normal activity.

docs.title: Step 2: Extract fields from raw XML
docs.text:
The log was ingested as raw XML with no field parsing, so I extracted SourceImage with rex and narrowed to Event ID 10:

index=botsv1 "lsass.exe" "<EventID>10</EventID>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='SourceImage'>(?<SourceImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| stats count by SourceImage

Result: 750 events from 14 source processes. Atomic Red Team binaries stand out immediately, but this view still mixes in normal Windows processes.

docs.title: Step 3: Isolate who opened LSASS, and with what rights
docs.text:
Event ID 10 records the access mask (GrantedAccess). Reading LSASS memory requires PROCESS_VM_READ (0x0010), so masks like 0x1fffff (full access) and 0x1410 are what dumping looks like. Routine system access is usually 0x1400 or 0x1000.

index=botsv1 "<EventID>10</EventID>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='SourceImage'>(?<SourceImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='TargetImage'>(?<TargetImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='GrantedAccess'>(?<GrantedAccess>[^<]+)</Data>"
| where match(TargetImage, "(?i)\\\\lsass\.exe$")
| stats count by SourceImage GrantedAccess
| sort - count

Result: 163 processes opened LSASS directly. 108 were normal Windows processes with low access masks. 55 were not.

Stage Events What changed Keyword sweep 851 Any event mentioning lsass.exe Event ID 10 only 750 Process access events, LSASS as source or target LSASS as target 163 Something opened LSASS Benign baseline 108 svchost, wininit, csrss, services with low access masks Alerts 55 Non-system processes with memory-read access

docs.title: Step 4: Pivot to process creation and file events
docs.text:
Event ID 10 shows who touched LSASS but not the command line. To confirm intent I pivoted to Event ID 1 (process creation) and Event ID 11 (file creation), looking for the command lines and the dump files they wrote.

index=botsv1 ("<EventID>1</EventID>" OR "<EventID>11</EventID>")
  ("lsass" OR "comsvcs" OR "mimikatz" OR ".dmp")
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='CommandLine'>(?<CommandLine>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='TargetFilename'>(?<TargetFilename>[^<]+)</Data>"
| table _raw CommandLine TargetFilename

docs.title: Processes that read LSASS memory
docs.text: Source Process Access Count Host Assessment AppData\Local\Temp\644c305e-...d1d.exe 0x1fffff 38 dc-807 Malicious. Dropped by wce.exe (Windows Credentials Editor) and run as a SYSTEM service by services.exe procdump.exe / procdump64.exe 0x1fffff 6 both Malicious. procdump -ma lsass.exe wrote lsass_dump.dmp notprocdump.exe / notprocdump64.exe 0x1fffff 3 dc-262 Malicious. Renamed ProcDump to evade name-based rules Outflank-Dumpert.exe 0x1fffff 2 dc-807 Malicious. Direct syscall dumper, wrote dumpert.dmp rundll32.exe 0x1fffff, 0x1410 2 dc-807 Malicious. comsvcs.dll MiniDump, a living-off-the-land dump taskmgr.exe 0x1fffff, 0x1410 3 dc-262 Suspicious. Interactive admin session created lsass (2).DMP from Task Manager powershell.exe 0x1410 1 dc-807 Needs context. Occurred 1 second after LSASS started at boot, before the attack chain

docs.title: Dump files written to disk (Event ID 11)
docs.text: Time (UTC) Host Writer File 2020-11-03 15:52:59 dc-807 procdump64.exe C:\Windows\Temp\lsass_dump.dmp 2020-11-03 15:53:03 dc-807 rundll32.exe ...\AppData\Local\Temp\lsass-comsvcs.dmp 2020-11-03 15:53:03 dc-807 Outflank-Dumpert.exe C:\Windows\Temp\dumpert.dmp 2021-02-03 16:51:01 dc-262 procdump64.exe C:\Windows\Temp\lsass_dump.dmp 2021-02-03 16:51:14 dc-262 notprocdump64.exe C:\Windows\Temp\lsass_dump.dmp 2021-02-03 21:34:57 dc-262 taskmgr.exe ...\AppData\Local\Temp\2\lsass (2).DMP

docs.title: Attack timeline: win-dc-807, 2020-11-03 (UTC)
docs.text:
Time Activity 15:52:48 PowerShell checks that dumping tools exist on disk (Test-Path ...\procdump.exe, mimikatz.exe) 15:52:58 wce.exe drops a GUID-named binary to Temp, which runs as a SYSTEM service and opens LSASS 38 times 15:52:59 procdump -accepteula -ma lsass.exe writes a full memory dump 15:53:03 rundll32 comsvcs.dll MiniDump and Outflank-Dumpert.exe each write a dump 15:53:03 mimikatz.exe "sekurlsa::minidump %tmp%\lsass.DMP" "sekurlsa::logonpasswords full" parses a dump offline 15:53:06 Cleanup: del lsass_dump.dmp, del dumpert.dmp, Remove-Item lsass-comsvcs.dmp

Key observation: Mimikatz never touched live LSASS. It parsed a dump file offline, so it does not appear in Event ID 10 at all. Only process creation logging (Event ID 1) caught it. A detection built only on Event ID 10 would miss this step.

docs.title: Indicators
docs.text: Type Value SHA256 7234C8F98B87593641BBDB594E34C94B9436986C4FB70E7DA5BCECFF147D14C3 (Temp service binary) MD5 605560CA0624AABF9F53675257B9BE21 File path C:\Users\ADMINI~1\AppData\Local\Temp\644c305e-30f4-470b-b616-d924c3206d1d.exe Tool directory C:\AtomicRedTeam\atomics\T1003.001\bin\ Dump files lsass_dump.dmp, lsass-comsvcs.dmp, dumpert.dmp, lsass (2).DMP Account ATTACKRANGE\Administrator

docs.title: 5. Detection Rule
docs.text:
Built to catch the behavior, not the tool name: any non-system process opening LSASS with memory-read rights.

index=botsv1 "<EventID>10</EventID>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='SourceImage'>(?<SourceImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='TargetImage'>(?<TargetImage>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Data Name='GrantedAccess'>(?<GrantedAccess>[^<]+)</Data>"
| rex field=_raw "<Computer>(?<host_name>[^<]+)</Computer>"
| where match(TargetImage, "(?i)\\\\lsass\.exe$")
| where match(GrantedAccess, "(?i)^0x(1fffff|1010|1410|1438|143a|1f3fff)$")
| where NOT match(SourceImage, "(?i)^C:\\\\Windows\\\\System32\\\\(svchost|wininit|csrss|services|lsm)\.exe$")
| eval severity=if(match(SourceImage, "(?i)\\\\(AppData|Temp|Users\\\\Public)\\\\"), "critical", "high")
| stats count min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen values(GrantedAccess) as access by host_name SourceImage severity
| sort - count

docs.title: Validation against the lab data
docs.text:
Metric Result LSASS access events evaluated 163 Alerts fired 55 Alerts tied to confirmed dumping 54 Alerts needing analyst context 1 (PowerShell at boot) Benign system accesses alerted 0 of 108 Renamed notprocdump.exe caught Yes, matched on behavior, not name

A Sigma version is in the detection library for porting to other SIEMs.

docs.title: 6. Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Detect the access mask, not the filename. notprocdump.exe would slip past a rule looking for "procdump". It cannot hide its 0x1fffff request to LSASS.
  2. Event ID 10 alone is not enough. Offline parsing with Mimikatz only shows up in process creation logs. Pair access monitoring with command line monitoring for sekurlsa, MiniDump, and -ma lsass.
  3. Watch for dump files. An Event ID 11 rule for *.dmp files containing "lsass" is a cheap second layer that caught every dump here, including the Task Manager one.
  4. Check your timestamps. Splunk set _time to my ingest time because the raw XML was not timestamp-parsed. The real event times came from the SystemTime field. In production, configure TIME_PREFIX in props.conf so timelines are correct.

docs.title: 7. Response Actions
docs.text:
• Isolate win-dc-807 and win-dc-262 from the network.
  • Reset passwords for every account with an active session on both hosts, starting with ATTACKRANGE\Administrator.
  • Reset the krbtgt account twice to invalidate forged Kerberos tickets.
  • Hunt for the SHA256 above and for *.dmp files across all endpoints.
  • Enable LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) and Credential Guard on domain controllers.

docs.title: Lab 04: Inbound Phishing Analysis and Header Forensics
docs.text:
Category: Phishing Triage ATT&CK: T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment | T1566.002 Spearphishing Link | TA0001 Initial Access Tools: Raw header analysis (RFC 5322), CyberChef, URL defanging, static document review Samples: TryHackMe Phishing Analysis module (training samples, analysis and write-up are my own)

Verdict: All samples malicious | Block, purge, and hunt for clicks

Every sample impersonated a known brand and either harvested credentials or delivered a payload. None should reach a user inbox.

docs.title: 1. Objective
docs.text:
Phishing is still the most common way attackers get in. Modern lures use brand impersonation, lookalike names, and multi-stage redirects to get past email gateways.

The goal: triage reported emails the way a SOC queue would, check headers for sender spoofing, trace links and redirects, review attachments, and produce a clean IOC set for blocking.

docs.title: 2. Triage Summary
docs.text: Sample Lure Technique Verdict Action PayPal receipt Fake transaction Display name spoofing, foreign envelope sender Malicious Block sender domain, purge Netflix suspension Account on hold Typosquatted display name, PDF with a payment link to a non-Netflix domain Malicious Block sender, purge, check for clicks Shared-file lure Document waiting URL shortener, tracking pixel, multi-hop redirect to fake Outlook login Malicious Block domains, reset any user who clicked Apple billing Blank body, attachment only .dot template that pulls remote macros Malicious Block attachment type, hash hunt DHL delivery "Enable content" spreadsheet .xlsx lure designed to launch regasm.exe Malicious Block, hunt for regasm.exe from Office

docs.title: Phase 1: Headers and sender identity
docs.text:
The display name and the real sending address did not match in either brand-impersonation sample:

  • PayPal: Displayed service@paypal.com, but the envelope sender came from sultanbogor[.]com, a domain with no relationship to PayPal.
  • Netflix: Display name Netllx billing, with "fi" swapped for "ll" so it reads as Netflix at a glance. Sent from z99@musacombi[.]online. The body pushed an attached PDF whose "Update Payment Account" link pointed to a non-Netflix domain, padded with a real Netflix help link and an odd-format phone number to look legitimate.

Mail clients show the display name prominently and hide the routing path. That gap is what these lures depend on.

What I check in every header:

Header Why it matters From vs Return-Path A mismatch is the fastest spoofing signal Authentication-Results SPF, DKIM, and DMARC pass or fail for the claimed domain Received chain (read bottom up) The true origin server and any odd relays Reply-To Often points to an attacker inbox even when From looks clean

docs.title: Phase 2: Links, tracking pixels, and redirects
docs.text:
1. URL shortener. Links went through hxxps://is[.]gd/6oCJ4m to hide the real landing page from scanners.
  2. Tracking pixel. A 1x1 image (tracking.png on devret[.]xyz) told the attacker the mailbox was live and the email was opened.
  3. Redirect chain. Links bounced through lookalike file-sharing pages (Citrix → OneDrive → Adobe) before landing on a fake Microsoft Outlook login page built to harvest credentials.

docs.title: Phase 3: Attachments
docs.text:
When links get blocked, attackers switch to attachments:

  • Apple .dot template. Blank email body, just the attachment. Word templates can fetch macros from a remote server when opened, so the file looks clean until it runs.
  • DHL .xlsx. The spreadsheet told the user to click "Enable Content", the step that lets embedded code run and launch regasm.exe, a signed Windows binary attackers abuse to run payloads.

docs.title: 4. IOCs (defanged)
docs.text: Type Indicator Context Sender domain sultanbogor[.]com PayPal impersonation Sender address z99@musacombi[.]online Netflix impersonation Tracking domain hxxp://devret[.]xyz Tracking pixel host Short link hxxps://is[.]gd/6oCJ4m Hides credential harvesting page Attachment Apple_Receipt.dot Remote template macro loader Process regasm.exe launched by Excel Living-off-the-land execution

docs.title: 5. Response and Detection
docs.text:
Immediate response

  • Purge every sample from all mailboxes, not just the reporter's.
  • Block the sender domains, tracking domain, and short link at the gateway and proxy.
  • Search proxy logs for anyone who reached the short link or the fake Outlook page. Any hit means a password reset and session revoke for that user.

Hardening

  1. Enforce DMARC alignment. Quarantine or reject mail where the From domain fails SPF alignment or has no valid DKIM signature.
  2. Block risky attachment types from external senders: .dot, .dotm, .xltm, and macro-enabled Office files.
  3. Automate triage. Have SOAR parse reported .eml files, defang links, expand shorteners in a sandbox, and check every domain against threat intel.

Endpoint detection for the DHL sample

index=sysmon EventCode=1
| where match(ParentImage, "(?i)\\\\(excel|winword)\.exe$")
    AND match(Image, "(?i)\\\\regasm\.exe$")
| table _time host User ParentImage Image CommandLine

docs.title: Lab 05: Windows Authentication & Brute Force Detection in Microsoft Sentinel (KQL)
docs.text:
Category: Cloud SIEM & Identity Detection Engineering ATT&CK: T1110.001 Password Guessing | T1110.003 Password Spraying | TA0006 Credential Access Platform: Microsoft Sentinel / Azure Log Analytics Workspace Telemetry: Windows Security Event Log (Event IDs 4625, 4624 via Azure Monitor Agent) Rule Format: Kusto Query Language (KQL)

Verdict: True Positive — High Severity — Account Compromised

Target host FIN-WKSTN-04 registered 142 failed network authentication attempts (Event ID 4625, SubStatus 0xC000006A) across a 12-minute window from source endpoint 192.168.10.45, followed immediately by a successful logon (Event ID 4624) under domain account CORP\jdoe. Immediate containment executed.

docs.title: 1. Investigation Scope & Objectives
docs.text:
Adversaries systematically deploy automated dictionary attacks and password spraying against network authentication interfaces to acquire valid enterprise credentials.

This investigation focused on: 1. Ingesting Windows Security event telemetry into an Azure Log Analytics Workspace via Azure Monitor Agent (AMA). 2. Analyzing diagnostic status codes within Event ID 4625 to differentiate account lockouts from invalid credentials. 3. Constructing an analytics rule in KQL that correlates anomalous bursts of failed logons followed by a successful logon event within a short timeframe.

docs.title: 2. Windows Authentication Telemetry
docs.text: Event ID Description Critical Correlation Fields 4625 An account failed to log on TargetUserName, LogonType, SubStatus, IpAddress, WorkstationName 4624 An account successfully logged on TargetUserName, LogonType, TargetLogonId, IpAddress, Computer

docs.title: Diagnostic Failure Sub-Status Codes
docs.text:
• 0xC000006A: STATUS_WRONG_PASSWORD (Username exists; credential guess was incorrect).
  • 0xC000006D: STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE (General failure or invalid username).
  • 0xC0000072: STATUS_ACCOUNT_DISABLED (Account is administratively disabled).
  • 0xC0000234: STATUS_ACCOUNT_LOCKED_OUT (Consecutive failures exceeded threshold).

docs.title: 3. Incident Timeline
docs.text: Timestamp (UTC) Event ID User Source IP Logon Type Diagnostic Code Finding 14:02:11 - 14:14:05 4625 (x142) CORP\jdoe 192.168.10.45 3 (Network) 0xC000006A High-frequency password guessing. 14:14:28 4624 CORP\jdoe 192.168.10.45 3 (Network) N/A Successful authentication. 14:15:10 4688 CORP\jdoe Local Host N/A N/A Discovery: whoami /all executed.

docs.title: 4. Detection Engineering: Microsoft Sentinel Analytics Rule (KQL)
docs.text: ```kql let timeRange = 1h; let failureThreshold = 10; let failedLogons = SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated >= ago(timeRange) | where EventID == 4625 | where SubStatus == "0xc000006a" | where isnotempty(IpAddress) and IpAddress != "-" and IpAddress != "127.0.0.1" | summarize FailureCount = count(), FirstFailure = min(TimeGenerated), LastFailure = max(TimeGenerated) by TargetAccount, IpAddress, Computer; let successfulLogons = SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated >= ago(timeRange) | where EventID == 4624 | where isnotempty(IpAddress) and IpAddress != "-" and IpAddress != "127.0.0.1" | project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, TargetAccount, IpAddress, Computer, LogonType; failedLogons | where FailureCount >= failureThreshold | join kind=inner (successfulLogons) on TargetAccount, IpAddress, Computer | where SuccessTime between (LastFailure .. (LastFailure + 10m)) | project FirstFailure, LastFailure, SuccessTime, TargetAccount, Computer, SourceIpAddress = IpAddress, FailureCount, LogonType | order by SuccessTime desc
